sents.t: One morning, Rosa came to my door holding an official envelope.
“I’ve been called for jury duty,” she said.
“I have to go to the courthouse next Monday.”
In America, citizens can be chosen to sit on a jury and decide if a person is guilty or not guilty.
It’s an important duty, and employers have to give workers the day off.
“Have you ever done it before?” I asked.
“Once, twenty years ago. It was a case about a stolen car.”
On Monday, Rosa spent the whole day at the courthouse.
Lawyers asked many people questions, and in the end, Rosa was chosen for a three-day trial.
She couldn’t tell me anything about the case until it was over.
Every evening, she just said, “It’s hard to decide someone’s future.”
When the trial ended, we talked over dinner.
“If I were on a jury,” I said, “I would be too nervous to decide.”
“You’d be good at it,” she said.
But only American citizens can serve on a jury.
“If I were a citizen, I could also vote,” I said.
“Then maybe one day you’ll become one.” For the first time, I seriously thought about it.
